content: The Lactational Amenorrhea Method (LAM) is a natural contraceptive approach that relies on the natural postpartum infertility experienced by women who are fully breastfeeding and remain amenorrheic. This method is considered a form of natural family planning when not combined with artificial chemicals or devices. For LAM to be effective, certain criteria must be met. During the first six months postpartum, LAM is approximately 98% effective if: Breastfeeding is the infant's sole or nearly sole source of nutrition. The introduction of formula, pumping instead of direct nursing, or feeding solids diminishes the effectiveness of LAM. The infant breastfeeds at least every four hours during the day and every six hours at night. The infant is less than six months old. The woman has not experienced a menstrual period after 56 days postpartum. Bleeding before 56 days postpartum is not considered indicative of fertility. Ecological breastfeeding, a stricter form of LAM developed by Sheila Kippley, has been shown to have a 1% failure rate in the first six months postpartum and a 6% failure rate before the return of the woman’s first postpartum menstruation. This method adheres to the Seven Standards of ecological breastfeeding, which include: Breastfeeding as the infant's only source of nutrition, with no formula, pumping, or solids (if the infant is under six months old). Pacifying the infant at the breast rather than using pacifiers or bottles. Frequent breastfeeding, with no scheduled feedings, as more frequent nursing enhances effectiveness. Mothers sleeping with their infants, either in the same bed or at least in the same room. Mothers avoiding separation from their infants for more than three hours per day. Mothers taking daily naps with their infants. The woman not experiencing a menstrual period after 56 days postpartum, with earlier bleeding disregarded. The return of fertility after childbirth varies significantly among individuals. Women who closely follow the Seven Standards of ecological breastfeeding tend to experience a delayed return of their menstrual cycles. On average, menstruation resumes around 14 months postpartum for women adhering to all seven criteria, though reports range from as early as two months to as late as 42 months. The first postpartum cycle is often anovulatory, reducing the likelihood of pregnancy before the first postpartum period. However, subsequent cycles are typically ovulatory and should be considered fertile. In some cases, breastfeeding may continue to interfere with fertility even after ovulation resumes. For example, luteal phases may be too short to sustain a pregnancy. Couples aiming for a spacing of 18 to 30 months between children can often achieve this through breastfeeding alone.
